'''Alison Grant Harcourt''' {{post-nominals|country=AUS|AO}} ({{nee|'''Doig'''}}; born 24 November 1929)<ref name="gradwomen">{{cite web |title=Alison Grant Harcourt |url=http://gradwomenvic.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2015/12/Alison-Harcourt.pdf |publisher=Graduate Women Victoria |accessdate=8 October 2018 |archive-date=3 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190303175428/http://gradwomenvic.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2015/12/Alison-Harcourt.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> is an Australian mathematician and statistician most well-known for co-defining the [[branch and bound]] algorithm along with [[Ailsa Land]] whilst carrying out research at the [[London School of Economics]].<ref name="abc">{{Cite news|url=http://www.abc.net.au/news/2018-10-08/meet-alison-harcourt-the-grandmother-of-australian-mathematics/10350170|title='I've always loved numbers': Meet the ground-breaking grandmother of Australian mathematics|date=2018-10-08|work=[[ABC News (Australia)|ABC News]]|access-date=2018-10-08|language=en-AU}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.gizmodo.com.au/2018/06/88-year-old-statistics-pioneer-says-some-barriers-for-women-in-stem-havent-changed-since-the-60s/|title=88 Year Old Statistics Pioneer Says Some Barriers For Women In STEM 'Haven't Changed Since The 60's'|date=2018-06-18|work=Gizmodo Australia|access-date=2018-10-08|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.lse.ac.uk/newsletters/pressAndInformation/staffNews/2010/20100218.htm|title=Staff News|website=[[London School of Economics]]|access-date=2018-10-08}}</ref> She was also part of the team which developed a [[poverty line]] as part of the Henderson Inquiry into [[poverty in Australia]] and helped to introduce the double randomisation method of ordering candidates used in Australian elections.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ms.unimelb.edu.au/news/alison-harcourt-received-doctor-of-science-honoris-causa|title=Alison Harcourt receives Doctor of Science (honoris causa)|last=Cashin|first=Kasey|date=2018-10-24|website=School of Mathematics and Statistics|language=en|access-date=2019-03-22}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Harcourt was born Alison Doig in [[Colac, Victoria]], in 1929. Her father was [[Keith Doig]], a physician and Australian rules footballer who received the [[Military Cross]] during [[World War I]]. Her mother, Louie Grant, was of Scottish descent and was sister to physicist Sir [[Kerr Grant]].<ref>[https://lbc.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/Profile-Feb-March19-web.pdf Richard and Alison Harcourt profile]</ref>

She was schooled at Colac West State School, Colac High School and [[Fintona Girls' School]].<ref name="gradwomen" /> After her schooling, she enrolled at the [[University of Melbourne]], gaining a [[Bachelor of Arts]] with a major in mathematics, and then a [[Bachelor of Science]] majoring in physics. While specialising in statistics undertaking a [[Master of Arts]] degree, she developed a technique for [[integer linear programming]].<ref name="gradwomen" />

==London School of Economics==
On the basis of her work in linear programming, she started work at the [[London School of Economics]] (LSE) in the late 1950s. In 1960, Doig and fellow LSE mathematician [[Ailsa Land]], published a landmark paper in the economics journal ''[[Econometrica]]'' ("An Automatic Method for Solving Discrete Programming Problems"), which outlined a [[branch and bound]] optimisation algorithm for solving [[NP-hard]] problems.<ref name="gradwomen" /><ref name="land_doig">{{cite journal|title=An automatic method of solving discrete programming problems|author=A. H. Land and A. G. Doig|journal=Econometrica|year=1960|issue=3|volume=28|pages=497–520|doi=10.2307/1910129|jstor=1910129}}</ref> The algorithm is the backbone idea behind all modern [[Integer programming]] solvers such as [[Gurobi]], [[Cplex]].<ref name="abc" />

==University of Melbourne==
In 1963, Doig returned to Melbourne, where she took up a position as a senior lecturer in statistics at the University of Melbourne.<ref name="abc" />

In the mid-1960s, she joined a team headed by the sociologist Ronald Henderson which was attempting to quantify the extent of [[poverty in Australia]]. The team developed the Henderson Poverty Line in 1973, which was the disposable income required to support the basic needs of a family of two adults and two dependent children. The techniques developed by the Henderson team have been used by the [[Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic and Social Research]] to regularly update the [[poverty line]] for Australia since 1979.<ref name="gradwomen" />

In 1970, Harcourt took study leave in Sweden, where she co-authored two papers on theoretical chemistry—"A simple demonstration of Hund’s Rule for the helium 2S and 2P States"<ref name="hunds-rule">{{cite journal |last1=Harcourt |first1=R.D. |last2=Harcourt |first2=Alison |title=A simple demonstration of the origin of hund's rule for the helium 2S and 2P states |journal=Chemical Physics |date=May 1973 |volume=1 |issue=3 |pages=238–243 |doi=10.1016/0301-0104(73)85018-9 |bibcode=1973CP......1..238H }}</ref> and "Wavefunctions for 4-electron 3-centre bonding"<ref name="3e4c">{{cite journal |last1=Harcourt |first1=Richard D. |last2=Harcourt |first2=Alison |title=Wavefunctions for "4-electron, 3-centre" bonding units |journal=J. Chem. Soc., Faraday Trans. 2 |date=1974 |volume=70 |pages=743–757 |doi=10.1039/F29747000743}}</ref>—with her husband, the chemist Richard Harcourt.<ref name="gradwomen" />

In 1975, following the [[1975 Australian constitutional crisis|dismissal of the Whitlam government]], Harcourt and fellow statistician Malcolm Clark noticed irregularities in the distribution of party ordering on the Senate ballot papers for the [[1975 Australian federal election|1975 federal election]] which was determined by drawing envelopes from a box, with [[Coalition (Australia)|Coalition parties]] holding one of the first two positions in every state. Harcourt and Clark made a submission to the Joint Select Committee on Electoral Reform, which resulted in a 1984 amendment to the ''[[Commonwealth Electoral Act 1918|Commonwealth Electoral Act]]'' to introduce a more rigorous double randomisation method.<ref name="amsi">{{cite web |title=Election ballots (Australian Senate, 1975) |url=http://amsi.org.au/ESA_Senior_Years/SeniorTopic4/4a/4a_2content_6.html |publisher=Australian Mathematical Sciences Institute |accessdate=8 October 2018}}</ref> Harcourt and Clark published a paper about their analysis and recommendations for the ''Australian & New Zealand Journal of Statistics'' in 1991.<ref name="senate">{{cite journal |last1=CLARK |first1=R.M. |title=Randomisation and the 1975 Senate Ballot Draw |last2=HARCOURT |first2=A.G. |journal=Australian Journal of Statistics |date=September 1991 |volume=33 |issue=3 |pages=261–278 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-842X.1991.tb00433.x}}</ref>

Harcourt retired as an academic from the University of Melbourne in 1994, but continued to work there as a sessional tutor in statistics.<ref name="gradwomen" /> She finally retired completely aged 90 in 2019.<ref name="rss">{{cite journal |volume=22|issue=1|title=Living long and prospering: Alison Harcourt |journal=Significance |date=January 2025 |pages=44–45 |publisher=Royal Statistical Society}}</ref> She pointed out in an interview that she had "tutored or lectured in every decade from the 1940s to the 2010s".<ref name="rss"/>

In October 2018 Harcourt was named as 2019 [[Australian of the Year#Senior Australian of the Year|Senior Victorian Australian of the Year]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.triplem.com.au/news/bendigo/bendigo-dr-skye-kinder-victorian-young-australian-of-the-year |title=Bendigo Dr Skye Kinder Victorian Young Australian of the Year |date=24 October 2018 |publisher=[[Triple M Bendigo]] |accessdate=25 October 2018}}</ref> In early December 2018, the University of Melbourne awarded Harcourt with an honorary Doctor of Science degree.<ref name="dsc">{{cite news |last1=Dodd |first1=Tim |title=Six decades on, unsung pioneer Alison Harcourt honoured |url=https://www.theaustralian.com.au/higher-education/computing-pioneer-to-receive-honorary-phd/news-story/3d84bb398a865a83c252ee7c5edff372 |accessdate=8 November 2018 |work=[[The Australian]]|date=7 November 2018}}</ref>

In June 2019, Harcourt was made an [[Officer of the Order of Australia]] in recognition of her "distinguished service to mathematics and computer science through pioneering research and development of integer linear programming".<ref>{{cite web|last=|first=|date=June 10, 2019|title=Award: Officer of the Order of Australia|url=https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/2004790|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200318121747/https://honours.pmc.gov.au/honours/awards/2004790 |archive-date=18 March 2020 |accessdate=October 12, 2020|website=Australian Honours|publisher=Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet}}</ref>
